abstract: We prove two new local results for biplanar graphs. First, if a six-clique Q has degree at most nine at every vertex and three distinct common neighbors, with arbitrary edges among them and arbitrary fourth neighbors, then deleting Q admits an ambient biplanar reduction whose every proper nine-coloring lifts. The proof reduces failed palettes to a connected/disconnected two-layer residual and closes 22,804 complete variable-slot cases with literal K5/K3,3 subdivisions; it imports the published mandatory four-terminal attachment theorem. Second, we give a twelve-vertex, 40-edge, exactly eight-chromatic biplanar control with two common neighbors for which terminal edges routed through Q and nonadjacent pair identifications cannot universally extend nine-colorings in the supplied layers. The obstruction survives completing each active boundary to a clique and replacing Q by at most five fresh vertices while retaining the six distinct exterior vertices and their exterior-edge restriction. These results distinguish an ambient reduction from a private-routing barrier; they neither establish irreducibility for all two-common configurations nor provide a ten-chromatic graph or an occurrence theorem. Exact rotations, a standard-library checker and compact evidence are supplied.

change_summary: Retain accepted Sections 2–18 and Appendices A/B from version 3. Add peer-audited Theorem 27: a degree-at-most-nine private K6 with three arbitrary common terminals and arbitrary fourth neighbors admits an ambient biplanar nine-color extension reduction. Add Proposition 28: a literal twelve-vertex, 40-edge, exactly eight-chromatic two-common control defeats the specified Q-internal routing and identification class, including the at-most-five fresh-vertex replacement; explicitly state that the six exterior vertices remain distinct. Add the complete standard-library residual certificate and supporting geometry controls, record the corrected singleton-terminal subdivision, credit the independent audit, retain the explicit Paper 25 premise, and state that neither result is an occurrence theorem or a global irreducibility theorem. Qualify the new checker as Python 3.10+ and preserve the exact compact supplement.

coauthors.contribution: Identified the singleton-terminal gap in the new common-triple reduction, independently supplied the explicit K3,3 subdivision repair, replayed the complete residual certificate and hand controls, and audited the final hand reduction. The author developed the theorem, its coverage argument and the two-common routing control.
